mainText: Good morning. Here is your curated AI briefing for Saturday, October 24, 2026. Block has introduced a new voice model named Dessa, developed by the company’s research lab. The model is notable for its ability to generate human-like expressions, including laughter, pauses, and signs of fatigue or emotion, without relying on text-based voice tags. By avoiding the use of explicit voice tags, which are common in models like ElevenLabs v4 or Fish Audio Drama 3, Dessa aims to create a more natural, immersive, and responsive conversational experience. According to the company, the model is fully trained on human speech and functions as a full-duplex system, meaning it can process input and output simultaneously, similar to OpenAI’s GPT-Live. Block emphasizes that current voice AI can feel unnatural and may miss non-verbal cues, which can lead to a degraded user experience. Because the model is designed to run locally on consumer-grade hardware, specifically the MacBook M4 Max or higher, it offers the potential for cost-effective, private, and powerful voice interactions. While this could eventually power expanded business and consumer experiences for companies like Square, Block has not provided public access to Dessa. Instead, the firm is issuing a call for safety researchers to evaluate the model for potential risks, such as the possibility of the voice agent being used to impersonate others or deceive users in automated interactions. In the policy sector, OpenAI announced that it has implemented a new security protocol for its frontier model training environment. The company stated that, based on current alignment research and the state of internet infrastructure security, it is now conducting all frontier model training without internet access. This move serves to strengthen containment and security boundaries around the development of the most powerful AI systems. OpenAI noted that this restriction will remain in place until future advancements in safety safeguards and monitoring systems justify a change in policy. In a separate development, a study conducted by researchers at Convovo, led by Cornell professor Tapan Parikh, examined the political tendencies of AI models when prompted to make candidate recommendations. The research found that when forced to choose in upcoming midterm elections, SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 favored Republican candidates in 92% of its responses, while OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol favored Democratic candidates in 97% of cases. Researchers noted that the models often prioritized different topics and relied on distinct sets of sources to justify these choices, with Grok frequently citing conservative outlets and GPT leaning on mainstream news organizations. An OpenAI spokesperson stated that the study tested developer APIs with explicit demands for a recommendation, noting that the consumer-facing version of ChatGPT is designed to remain objective and generally declines to provide such endorsements. While the researchers noted that developers may plug models into products that behave differently than the standard chat interfaces, the study highlights how underlying model values and source material selection can influence output. SpaceXAI did not comment on the findings. In infrastructure news, AWS has released a guide for orchestrating SageMaker AI endpoint auto-scaling using the AWS Cloud Development Kit. The documentation addresses a technical hurdle where updating endpoint configurations—such as instance types or environment variables—causes deployments to fail because the system attempts to update the endpoint while the auto-scaling target is still registered. AWS provides a solution using custom resources that automatically deregister the target before an update and re-register it once the endpoint reaches an in-service state, ensuring scaling policies remain intact without manual intervention. This automation prevents deployment failures and stack instability that previously required manual CLI intervention. Additionally, Amazon Quick Sight has expanded the capabilities of its layer maps to support point and line geometry types via GeoJSON files. This update allows users to visualize specific locations, such as store sites, or movement paths, such as flight routes, alongside existing support for regional polygons. Users can now upload files up to 100 megabytes and join them with metrics in a Quick Sight dataset to create interactive, location-based visualizations.
